newsitem.title: USA: Nobel winner asks U.S. to back East Timor vote.
newsitem.headline: Nobel winner asks U.S. to back East Timor vote.

text.p: Nobel Peace Prize co-winner Jose Ramos-Horta on Tuesday called on President Bill Clinton to step up the pressure on Indonesia and endorse a referendum in East Timor to determine its future.

He told a Congressional Human Rights Caucus hearing that human rights abuses have increased since he and Archbishop Carlos Belo won the Nobel Peace Prize last year and drew world attention to the Indonesian-ruled territory of East Timor.

"It has become worse with hundreds and hundreds of young people, including teenagers, being arrested. Some have been shot at random," he said as the panel reviewed enlarged, colour photographs of young men being tortured with electric prods.

Ramos-Horta, a self-exiled spokesman for the resistance in East Timor, told the panel about a 17-year-old boy who had his feet nailed to the floor after demonstrating against Indonesia's presence in the former Portuguese colony, occupied by Jakarta in 1975.

He praised the Clinton administration for raising human rights abuses with Indonesian leaders and for restricting small arms and armoured vehicle sales to its military, but said East Timor needed more help.
"The only alternative left is for the United States to call for a referendum under United Nations supervision," he said.
The United Nations has never recognised Indonesia's annexation of East Timor and still regards Portugal as the administering power.
Ramos-Horta said that if the referendum supported independence, his allies in the resistance would permit Indonesia to "disengage from East Timor in a way that would save face."

He disputed Indonesia's claim that less than 6,000 troops are stationed in East Timor, citing an Australian Foreign Ministry estimate that there were about 20,000 to control an estimated 750,000 people.
He said the Indonesian army recruits "Ninja" squads of local teenagers, paying them to disrupt demonstrations and provide cover for riot troops to intervene and make arrests.
"They don't have the popular support," he said. "Torture has become the preferred way to rule. Indonesia has denied using torture and accuses the demonstrators of provoking its troops.
The U.S. State Department, Amnesty International and other human rights groups have cited numerous cases of abuses.
